guide.summary: GitHub OAuth apps are self-serve. You register the app behind a login, get a client ID right away, and generate a client secret that is shown only once. No provider review step is documented. The real gates are on the user side: organizations that restrict OAuth app access limit you to their public resources until an owner approves, SAML SSO orgs need an active session, and flagged accounts cannot authorize at all. GitHub itself recommends GitHub Apps over OAuth apps, except when you need enterprise-level resources.
auth_alternatives: GitHub App: GitHub's recommended model, with fine-grained permissions, more control over repository access and short-lived tokens. Choose it unless you need enterprise-level resources, which is where an OAuth app is preferred.

OAuth app device flow: use it for agents or CLIs without a browser redirect. You must enable it in the app settings first, and verification code submissions are rate-limited to 50 per hour per application.

reasons_to_bring_own: Your own app name is what users see on the authorization screen, and what org owners see when they approve access.
GitHub recommends a GitHub App over an OAuth app for fine-grained permissions and short-lived tokens. You would need your own app to adopt that model.
Rate limit increases for OAuth apps are granted per app and apply to every token. If you need an increase, you need your own app.
You control token expiry settings, such as 8-hour expiring tokens with refresh, only on an app you own.
build_or_borrow.verdict: Use Composio managed auth to start; you do not need your own app yet because GitHub OAuth apps have no documented review gate and you can register your own in minutes later, though note GitHub itself recommends a GitHub App over an OAuth app unless you need enterprise-level resources.

prerequisites.text: A GitHub account. The developer settings page sits behind a login wall.
An application name, which is shown to users during authorization.
An Authorization callback URL where GitHub redirects users after they authorize.
End users must have a verified email address before they can authorize the app.
If you want the device flow, enable it in the app settings before use.

oauth.token_lifetime: Long-lived by default. If expiring tokens are enabled, or the offline_access scope is requested, the access token lasts 8 hours and the refresh token expires after 6 months without use. The authorization code expires after 10 minutes.
redirect_uri_rules: Register at least one redirect URI. You can add up to 10, and wildcard matching is optional: only enable it if you control every URL it could match.
Exchange the returned code at the token endpoint within 10 minutes.
PKCE works only with S256; plain is not supported.
The implicit grant is not supported.

blockers.text: Organizations that restrict OAuth app access give your app only their public resources until an owner approves it. When an application policy is active, only an owner can authorize the app.
blockers.workaround: Tell users that members can request approval from their org owner, and prepare a short explanation of what the app accesses for that owner.

blockers.text: Flagged or restricted accounts cannot authorize third-party OAuth apps, and retrying does not help while the restriction remains.
blockers.workaround: No app-side fix. Detect the failure and show a clear message instead of retrying.

blockers.text: Users in SAML SSO organizations need an active SAML session each time they authorize.
blockers.workaround: Tell users to sign in to their org's SSO before they start the connect flow.

blockers.text: Users with unverified email addresses cannot authorize OAuth apps.
blockers.workaround: Surface a message asking the user to verify their GitHub email, then retry.

app_specific_gotchas.text: The client secret is shown only once when generated and cannot be viewed again. Store it immediately.

GitHub caps tokens at ten per user/application/scope combination and limits token creation to ten per hour. Hitting the hourly limit forces a browser re-authorization prompt instead of revoking the oldest token.
Requesting the offline_access scope returns an expiring access token plus a refresh token even if the app is not configured for expiring tokens. Your code must handle refresh in that case.
Turning on expiring user tokens does not expire tokens already issued. Older long-lived tokens keep working.
github.com has no OIDC or OAuth discovery document. Hardcode the authorize and token endpoints.

scope_tiers.purpose: Get a refresh token so the agent can keep acting for the user without re-prompting
scope_tiers.action_label: Stay connected with an expiring token plus refresh token
scope_tiers.gate: No GitHub review for this scope is documented. Requesting it returns an 8-hour access token and a refresh token even if the app is not set to expiring tokens. The refresh token dies after 6 months unused.
scope_tiers.cheaper_alternative: Skip it and use the default long-lived OAuth app token. This is simpler, but the credential is riskier to hold.

scope_tiers.scope: Repository and organization access scopes (names not covered by the provided claims)
scope_tiers.purpose: Read or act on the user's repos and org resources
scope_tiers.action_label: Access the user's repositories and organization data
scope_tiers.gate: No GitHub-side review is documented. The real gate is per organization. If an org restricts OAuth app access and has not approved the app, only its public resources are reachable. When an org application policy is active, only an owner can authorize the app, and members can only request approval. Orgs without restrictions authorize the app automatically.
scope_tiers.cheaper_alternative: GitHub recommends a GitHub App instead, for fine-grained permissions, repo-level control and short-lived tokens. Stay on an OAuth app only if you need enterprise-level resources.

paths.verdict: Low cliff. Once registered, any GitHub user can authorize the app. The provided claims document no GitHub app review. The only waiting is org owner approval, for orgs that restrict OAuth apps, and its duration is not documented. Choose OAuth App vs GitHub App before you build. No marketplace or internal-only mode is covered by the claims.

Per-org approval: an owner of each org that restricts OAuth apps must approve before private org resources are reachable. Members can request it. This is not a GitHub review, and its duration is not documented.

steps.title: Decide: OAuth App or GitHub App
steps.detail_md:
This is the developer's call; the agent can only lay out the trade-off.

- GitHub recommends building a GitHub App instead of an OAuth app (c25), because GitHub Apps use fine-grained permissions, give more control over repository access, and use short-lived tokens (c26).
- An OAuth app is preferred when the agent needs enterprise-level resources (c27).

This guide covers the OAuth app path. If you do not need enterprise-level resources, consider the GitHub App route before you continue. Composio lists a managed-auth GitHub toolkit, which could be an alternative to registering your own app. Its details are not covered by the claims here.

steps.title: Draft the registration form values
steps.detail_md:
The agent prepares these values for the developer to paste into the form:

- **Application name** (required). Users see it during authorization, so use your product name (c3).
- **Homepage URL** (required) (c4).
- **Application description** (optional) (c5).
- **Authorization callback URL** (required). GitHub redirects users here after they authorize, so it must match your backend's callback route (c6).

steps.title: Log in and register the OAuth app
steps.detail_md:
The registration pages sit behind a GitHub login (c39).

1. Go to Settings, then Developer settings, then OAuth Apps, then click **New OAuth App** (c2). The direct form is at github.com/settings/applications/new (c1).
2. Paste the values from step 2 and submit.
3. GitHub shows the client ID on registration, at the top of the app settings page (c1, c7).

No provider review or approval step for registering an OAuth app is documented in the claims.

steps.title: Generate the client secret and store it immediately
steps.detail_md:
1. On the app settings page, click the button that generates a client secret (c7).
2. Copy it straight into your secret manager.

GitHub shows the secret only once and you cannot view it again (c7, c8). If you lose it, you will have to generate a new one.

steps.title: Choose token expiry and device flow settings
steps.detail_md:
**Expiring user tokens**

- This setting is optional (c10).
- By default, tokens are long-lived (c21, c33).
- With expiry on, the access token lasts 8 hours and the refresh token expires after 6 months without use (c32).
- Turning it on later does not expire tokens that already exist (c10).
- Requesting the `offline_access` scope yields an expiring token plus a refresh token even when the setting is off (c35).

**Device flow**

- Only enable it if your agent runs where a browser redirect is awkward (CLI, headless). It must be enabled in the app settings before use (c9, c36).

The recommendation for an agent is to enable expiring tokens, so a leaked token has limited life.

steps.title: Write the OAuth flow code
steps.detail_md:
**Endpoints**

- Authorize: `GET https://github.com/login/oauth/authorize` (c28).
- Token exchange: `POST https://github.com/login/oauth/access_token` (c29, c11).
- Device flow, if enabled: `https://github.com/login/device/code` (c36).
- Hardcode these. github.com has no OIDC or OAuth discovery document (c40, c41).

**Flow rules**

- Use the authorization code grant. Implicit is not supported; device grant is the alternative (c30).
- Use PKCE with `S256` only. `plain` is rejected (c31).
- Exchange the code promptly, because it expires after 10 minutes (c11, c34).

Scope names for your use case are not covered by the claims. Pick them from GitHub's scope docs.

steps.title: Handle token limits and refresh
steps.detail_md:
**Token reuse**

- GitHub caps tokens at ten per user/application/scope combination and limits creation to ten per hour (c15).
- Store and reuse tokens instead of re-running the flow.
- Hitting the hourly limit sends the user to a re-authorization prompt in the browser. It does not revoke the oldest token (c16).

**Refresh and rate limits**

- If you enabled expiry or request `offline_access`, refresh the access token before its 8 hours run out, and track refresh-token idle time (c32, c35).
- Device flow verification submissions are limited to 50 per hour per application (c12, c38).
- Rate limit increases, if granted, are per app and apply to every token (c24). The process for getting one is not documented here.

steps.title: Add clear user-facing errors for account and org blockers
steps.detail_md:
Detect these cases and tell the user what to do.

**Account blockers**

- **Unverified email:** the user must verify their email before authorizing (c13).
- **Flagged or restricted account:** the user cannot authorize, and retrying will not help while the restriction remains (c14).
- **SAML SSO orgs:** the user needs an active SAML session each time they authorize (c19).

**Organization access**

- If an org restricts OAuth app access and has not approved your app, you only reach its public resources (c17).
- Orgs without restrictions authorize the app automatically (c18).
- Under an org application policy, only an org owner can authorize. Members can request approval (c23). Tell users to ask their owner.

steps.title: Test end to end with your own GitHub account
steps.detail_md:
1. Log in and run the full authorize, callback and token exchange with the real client ID.
2. A bad or unknown client ID still lands on the GitHub sign-in page rather than an obvious error (c42), so verify success by checking that a token comes back.
3. Test a private org repo to confirm org approval behaves as expected (c17, c23).

steps.title: Share the integration with users
steps.detail_md:
Once testing passes, users can connect.

- No provider-side app review, approval queue or user cap for OAuth apps is documented in the claims, so there is no GitHub review wait to plan for.
- The real gate is per organization. Org owners may need to approve your app before your agent can reach private org resources (c17, c23).
- How long an owner takes is outside GitHub's documentation and outside your control.

drivers: org owner approval when OAuth app access is restricted
per-user token cap and hourly creation limit

belief_diff.topic: Does letting arbitrary users connect require provider review or verification?
belief_diff.prior_belief: No, GitHub OAuth apps let any GitHub user authorize the app immediately without any review or verification by GitHub.
belief_diff.finding: The claims do not say GitHub reviews OAuth apps, but they do show user-level verification and restrictions: users must verify their email before authorizing, flagged or restricted accounts cannot authorize third-party apps, and organization owners can gate app authorization under an application policy.

belief_diff.prior_belief: There is no approval process for GitHub OAuth apps, so the wait time is zero seconds, as apps are active upon registration.
belief_diff.finding: The claims do not address app registration wait time. They only describe organization approval requests for installing an app into an organization, which is a different process.

belief_diff.topic: Limits while the app is unapproved
belief_diff.prior_belief: GitHub OAuth apps have no unapproved state, so there are no restrictions on users or rate limits beyond the standard API rate limit of 5,000 requests per hour per user.
belief_diff.finding: The claims contradict the claim of no unapproved state: if an organization restricts OAuth app access and does not approve the app, it can reach only that organization's public resources. Token creation is capped at ten per user/app/scope and ten per hour, and the 5,000 requests per hour figure is not stated in the claims.

belief_diff.prior_belief: Registering and running a GitHub OAuth app is free, with no fees of any amount required.
belief_diff.finding: The claims do not mention fees or pricing for registering or running an OAuth app.

belief_diff.topic: Key prerequisites (domain, privacy policy, video, business verification)
belief_diff.prior_belief: No domain, privacy policy, demo video, or business verification is required; you only need a GitHub account and an application name, homepage URL, and callback URL.
belief_diff.finding: The form fields match: an application name, a Homepage URL, and an Authorization callback URL are required, and description is optional. The claims do not say whether a domain, privacy policy, video, or business verification is required or not. They add that users must verify their email address before authorizing, which the prior omitted.

belief_diff.prior_belief: The authorization callback URL must match the registered callback URL's host and port, and the redirect_uri parameter may be a subpath of the registered callback URL, but GitHub Apps differ in allowing multiple callback URLs.
belief_diff.finding: The claims do not address redirect_uri matching rules, subpath behavior, or whether GitHub Apps allow multiple callback URLs. They only say the form requires an authorization callback URL where users are redirected after authorizing.
